items.body: Shell and Core takes its title from the unfinished concrete structures that have become fixtures of the Syrian landscape, and Tasgeelat Al-Husni تسجيلات الحُسني uses that image of arrested construction as a way of looking at lives left incomplete. Much of the record is assembled from things heard or observed in everyday life: bureaucratic rituals, checkpoints, cars, street conversations, scrap collectors and an uncle’s absurd political opinions. On “Spacetune” these details accumulate into a comic story that deliberately goes nowhere; “Existing” turns repetition and waiting into its subject, while the heavier “Grinder” pushes familiar material towards something more grotesque. The humour is important. Rather than presenting Syria exclusively through catastrophe, Tasgeelat Al-Husni draws on a local tradition of satire and everyday mockery in which absurdity is one means of living with circumstances that have themselves become absurd. The music operates in much the same way, refusing a clean division between local tradition and experimental electronics. The oud can introduce the relatively spacious “Existing”, sit behind electronic and guitar noise on “Spacetune”, or grind against doom-laden riffs on “Grinder”. Al-Husni explicitly rejects using the instrument as a nostalgic signifier of a disappearing culture; here it belongs to the present as naturally as synthesis, distortion or field recording. Progressive and heavy rock are equally embedded in the record’s vocabulary, particularly in its abrupt shifts between calm and physical weight. Lazar Mečanin’s production makes those contrasts unusually pronounced: passages of relative openness can suddenly thicken into distortion, low-frequency pressure and noise, giving the album the unstable logic of the environment it describes. One of the album’s most striking changes of register comes on “Perspective”, where the voice of Ukrainian opera singer Oksana Vakula introduces a radiant tone, briefly opening up the record’s otherwise rough and unstable sonic terrain. That makes the unfinished Massar Discovery Center on the cover more than an illustration. Along with Syria’s other abandoned concrete shells, it becomes an architectural counterpart to a record about interrupted trajectories. Yet Shell and Core avoids turning incompletion into a grand metaphor. What matters most is the peripheral and the discarded: things overheard, jokes, irritating routines, incongruous sounds and surreal encounters. The picture of Syria that emerges is at the same time damaged and precarious, but also mundane and funny, a place whose exposed structural bones are filled with everyday life. To help us better understand the production process for Shell and Core we reached out directly to Tasgeelat Al-Husni. Throughout عَ العَضم (Shell and Core), everyday Syrian life is depicted in a way that often feels almost surreal, allowing the ordinary and the mythical to coexist. The repeated “unknown” in “Spacetune”, the taxi driver nicknamed Azrael—the Angel of Death—blasting heavy dabke, the endless bureaucracy of “Existing”, the Ladas, and finally the litany of scrap collectors all feel like fragments of the same social landscape. There is also a distinctly sardonic humour running through the writing. Do you think of your lyrics as poetry, documentary montage, social commentary or simply another way of composing with sound? Most of the lyrics are rephrasing of something I have heard in Syria either in a conversation with friends or randomly on the street. I wrote down some of what I had heard and then integrated them with how I thought of each song. I am new to writing words, so I don’t know much, but I have tried writing a comical story with mild suspense that leads nowhere on “Spacetune,” describing recurrent scenes from daily life on “Existing,” and creating some surreal visual scenes on “Grinder.” The sardonic humor is essential to the environment where the album came from. It’s in the music we hear (such as the music of the Rahbani family), the TV we watch (such as Spotlight – بقعة ضوء), the books we read (such as Muhammad al-Maghut’s), so you would also hear it in your day-to-day life from your relatives, your college friends, the bus driver or even from a soldier on a checkpoint. Add to that the absurdity of people’s takes on the conflict, like that uncle on Spacetune, which naturally calls for mockery. Peugeot 504 – photo by Hussain Hussain The second track, “Existing”, opens with an oud before gradually expanding into a much broader electronic landscape. The instrument never feels nostalgic or symbolic of tradition; instead, it becomes another texture within the composition. Was it important for you to avoid treating the oud as a marker of cultural identity, allowing it instead to coexist naturally with electronics and noise? It was! I think such instruments are not supposed to sound like a distant cry from the past echoing in an empty space, or “a ghostly remnant from a lost culture”, like David Byrne once wrote. The oud, like any instrument, should be used to serve the song the way the song is meant to be. It definitely could be used in its classical character with takasim and as accompaniment for singing like on “Existing,” but it can also accompany heavy doom metal riffs to add a bloody drilling texture on “Grinder,” or do some finger picking behind synth and guitar noises like on Spacetune. If you listen to a based folk performance from the past, you hear the oud vital and integrated with the rest of the instruments, not sounding like an anomaly, and I think this is how it should be treated in any other (modern) context. Window – photo by Hussain Hussain Although the album is rooted in electroacoustic composition and experimental electronics, there are moments—particularly in the treatment of distortion, low-frequency weight and rhythmic pressure—that recall progressive rock, heavy rock and noise. Are those traditions part of your musical vocabulary, and how do they intersect with the experimental and electronic music you make today? These traditions strongly influence how we have approached this record and music making in general. The treatment of sound at this level was more Lazar’s part, so I have forwarded the question to him, and this is his response: “Those traditions have to be a part of our vocabulary given the fact it’s the music we grew up on – Floyd, Crimson, etc. These bands influenced us as players but they also influenced how we think about music. A song can exhibit cinematic properties and sometimes be even more immersive than a movie if done right. The record is really a landscape representing every-day life in Syria (if I understood it correctly myself hah), moments of beauty and calmness intertwined with unpredictable chaos mostly right next to each other, so in a way the music is interpreting life, and by using these acoustic and production techniques we are attempting to recreate the feelings one might have simply living there.” Random Structure – photo by Hussain Hussain How do you see your work in relation to other Syrian experimental musicians? Is there a shared aesthetic or set of concerns emerging from the scene, or do you feel that each artist is responding to the experiences of recent years in fundamentally different ways? I have learned a lot from contemporary Syrian and Arab artists — Tootard, Shabjdeed, Khaled Allaf, Lynn Adib, Al-Rahel Al-Kabir, Kulna Sawa, and many more — and that has encouraged me to work on my own stuff, sing about what I have heard or seen, and eventually release that. It is true that everyone is responding to their experiences in their own way; some express that in a desperate way, some in a cynical way, some tackle social issues, and some speak about personal experiences. Maybe what we have in common is our frustration and disgust with our situation now and in recent years, but who knows? What’s important to me is that many of our artists sound so fresh, so unique and so relevant, and I always look forward to hearing their new approaches and what they are talking about. The cover features the unfinished Massar Discovery Center (“Massar Rose”) in Damascus—a project that was meant to embody education, innovation and the future before construction stopped in 2014. Throughout the album, there is a recurring sense of lives shaped by interruption: bureaucratic waiting, checkpoints, abandoned trajectories and systems that never quite reach completion. Did you see the building as encapsulating that condition, or were you drawn to it for different reasons? Gardenia Towers – photo by Hussain Hussain Exactly, hence the name, ع العضم Shell and Core! The rest of the album art (partly prepared for a CD release) features some well-known incomplete buildings, such as the infamous 50-year-old Yalbugha Tower in the middle of the capital and the Gardenia Towers in Homs that became known among the public as the “Death Towers”, used by snipers during the war. Such giant incomplete, mostly ugly, structures are so common to see in Syria. They are ironically reflective of the life of Syrian individual that has become so crippled, it might never reach a sense of completion. Everyone who lost their home forever and had to live in a tent, everyone that lost their beloved ones, got detained for the stupidest reason, or had to serve in the army for 8 years or so, and also everyone who just had to live or grow up there during these awful times. To me, this building not only encapsulates these incomplete trajectories, but also resembles, with its bare bones (عضم) sticking out, how naked, exposed and fragile we are. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以叙利亚未完成的混凝土建筑为意象，将官僚仪式、检查站、街巷对话和田野录音等日常素材拼贴为声音叙事。阿拉伯乌德琴与合成器、失真、噪音并存，既非怀旧符号也非单纯的实验素材，而是当代叙事的自然载体。制作上在开阔与低频压迫之间频繁切换，使音乐本身带有不稳定的环境逻辑，乌克兰歌剧女声的出现构成全作最鲜明的调性转折。专辑拒绝将叙利亚简化为灾难叙事，而是通过讽刺与荒诞——包括荒唐的政治言论与重复的等待——呈现一种地方性幽默如何在断裂中维持日常。残缺的结构、暴露的钢筋对应着被中断的人生轨迹，但音乐关注的核心始终是那些被忽略的、琐碎的、偶尔超现实的声音碎片。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张九碟套装是对韩国裔作曲家与即兴演奏家Jin Hi Kim四十年录音生涯的回顾性整理，由Neuma厂牌发行。Kim早年接受韩国传统音乐精英训练，赴美后转向电子音乐与作曲，师从Lou Harrison与Terry Riley，跨越东西方音乐传统的鸿沟。她将四世纪以来的韩国传统乐器杖琴通过计算机接口和信号处理大幅拓展其声音表现力，与Kronos Quartet、Derek Bailey等当代作曲与即兴领域的代表人物合作。套装均衡收录其创作与即兴作品：五张碟呈现管弦乐与室内乐创作，四张碟记录与Gerry Hemingway、Susie Ibarra、Tony Oxley、Bill Frisell等不同领域音乐家的即兴对话。Kim在回溯中重新发现自己早期将韩国音乐转译为西方乐器或使用图形记谱的实验，以及使用声音受限的传统乐器与国际大师级即兴演奏家对话的勇气。这套合集展现了一位音乐家持续跨界、融合传统与现代、亚洲与西方音乐语汇的完整轨迹。

items.body: This new release from the Belgian act Hybryds is a remarkable record. The title leaves little to the imagination, focusing—as the work of many artists across various disciplines has so often done—on the seven deadly sins. What makes this release particularly intriguing, however, is that four of the tracks date back to 2002, originally appearing on the “Lust”-EP released by Spectre. After all these years, the original singer, Miss Poly-Ester, got back in touch with Sandy Nijs and asked him to complete the album. So Sandy returned to the music, and the lost tracks were finally completed with the singer’s vocals. In total, we are treated to eleven tracks. Alongside the songs addressing the seven deadly sins, there are extras such as an intro and two live tracks dating from 2003. Hybryds has continued to surprise me in recent years. The project remains true to its trademark Ritualistic style, yet everything sounds more modern. This record stands out in particular for its slow, infectious, Trip-Hop-like rhythms. At times, I get the impression of hearing an Industrial version of Tricky—and that is very much intended as a huge compliment. After all, Hybryds naturally retains that familiar industrial DNA. The atmosphere remains dark, mysterious, and unsettling, evoking the feeling of stepping into a forbidden place where a certain decadence gradually sweeps you away. This impression is further reinforced by the artistic and highly explicit booklet accompanying the album, allowing Sandy Nijs to indulge his interest in and inspiration from fetish culture through a series of photographs that remain closely connected to the central theme. It is the kind of booklet that algorithms would rapidly detect and block instantly. Fortunately, there are still artists daring enough to go there—artists for whom it isn’t simply about nudity, provocation, or shock value. The music is far too good for that. I wouldn’t claim that Hybryds have reinvented themselves, but in recent years they have clearly been riding a new wave of inspiration, and this record is a fine example of where that has taken them. The older live tracks don’t exactly add much value, but the rest of the album is simply magnificent. As far as I’m concerned, it’s one of the best albums I’ve discovered this year. It would be a true sin to let this particular gem pass you by… (Ratring:9). Listen to “Envy”: Envy by Hybryds About Hybryds Hybryds is a Belgian project centered on Sandy Nys, active since the mid-1980s and known for ritual, mythical and industrial electronic work rooted in the cassette-era Belgian underground. Nys’ career began with the 1986 cassette “Mythical Music From The 21st Century,” followed by releases including “Music For Rituals” (1992) and “The Ritual Of The Rave” (1995). In the 1990s Hybryds became a duo with Leen Smets (Yasnaïa); from 2000 Nys continued the project solo before German vocalist Madeline joined, with multi-instrumentalist Peter De Koning later expanding the lineup. On 3RioArt / Zoharum, Hybryds has released “Mythopia” (2022), “Mythopia, The Sequel” (2024), “In The Wake Of The Witch” (2025), “Fire And Ice, Flesh And Bones Part 1 & 2” (2026) and “Desert Of White Salt” (2026). “7even Deadly Sins” follows on the same labels, reworking four tracks that originally appeared on the 2002 “Lust” EP on Spectre with new vocals by Madeline and Katherina.
items._cn_summary: 比利时项目 Hybryds 的新专辑围绕七宗罪主题展开，其中四首曲目源自 2002 年未完成的早期作品，经多年后由原主唱 Miss Poly-Ester 回归补录完成人声。整张专辑十一首曲目在保留其标志性的仪式感暗黑工业 DNA 基础上，融入了缓慢而具有传染力的 Trip-Hop 式节奏律动，呈现出工业化的 Tricky 式质感。整体氛围黑暗、神秘且令人不安，配合以恋物文化为灵感的极端视觉艺术手册，强化了禁忌与颓废的沉浸感。两首 2003 年的现场曲目价值有限，但其余作品在声音设计、节奏编排与概念统一性上表现出色，是该项目近年来灵感新阶段的代表之作。

items.album: John Coltrane 100: Exploring the Archives
items.excerpt: John Coltrane - One Down, One Up: Live At the Half Note (recorded 1965, released 2005), My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport (recorded 1963 and 1965, released 2007), Offering: Live At Temple University (recorded 1966, released 2014), A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle (recorded 1965, released 2021), Evenings At the Village Gate: John Coltrane with Eric Dolphy (recorded 1961, released 2023) By Lee Rice Epstein 1965 was remarkably transformative year in Coltrane’s history. Thankfully, through its
items.body: John Coltrane - One Down, One Up: Live At the Half Note (recorded 1965, released 2005), My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport (recorded 1963 and 1965, released 2007), Offering: Live At Temple University (recorded 1966, released 2014), A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle (recorded 1965, released 2021), Evenings At the Village Gate: John Coltrane with Eric Dolphy (recorded 1961, released 2023) By Lee Rice Epstein 1965 was remarkably transformative year in Coltrane’s history. Thankfully, through its ongoing archival releases, Impulse Records has continued to fill in the picture of how, as an artist, he continually pushed himself and his band, deeply and passionately giving his all at all times. One Down, One Up takes us right to March 26, 1965, where Coltrane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones play an astonishingly high-wire, high-energy “One Down, One Up” that runs nearly 30 minutes. The electricity crackling between players says exactly why Coltrane still matters, why he’s still adored, and why countless players of all kinds continue to study and revere him. The set’s recapitulation on the Newport stage months later (the second half of My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport ), more clearly shows how the group was thinking about and working through their headiest ideas. That the Newport set was released with a 1963 performance featuring Roy Haynes in the drummer seat gives some additional dimensions to the quartet’s changes over time. Tyner and Jones moved on by the next year, while Garrison held down the Alice Coltrane, Rashied Ali, and Pharoah Sanders group. Reportedly, he didn’t play with them in the fall of 1966, when Coltrane led a phenomenal set at Temple University. Offering has been alternately reviled and lauded, cited by some as a polished but unnecessary bootleg for completists only. But, if one just takes a step back and considers Offering happening the same season as Albert Ayler’s seminal European tour—with the quintet of Ayler, Donald Ayler, Michel Samson, Bill Folwell, and Beaver Harris—and if one wants to get really interested in sympathetic wavelengths, you hear Coltrane singing reportedly for the first time ever during “Leo” on November 11, 1966, while Ayler was recorded doing the same on a performance of Sanders’s “Japan” the previous night, November 10, 1966. That Ayler later screamed during his memorial performance for Coltrane would be too on the nose if someone manufactured it. The two shared both intellectual and spiritual bonds, a beautiful thing we’re scarcely able to know of or understand even partly. As the saying goes, it would have been enough to get these first three albums, but the 2020s has produced two seemingly impossible sessions: a live recording of “A Love Supreme,” also from 1965, and an unissued session with Eric Dolphy from 1961, featuring “Greensleeves” and “Africa.” What, truly can be said about Coltrane and Dolphy that doesn’t lead to a mountain of what-if or if-only hypotheticals? The hour-plus set is fiery and rich with ideas in motion. If someone told me this was 1963 or ’64, I wouldn’t doubt it. By ’61, both Coltrane and Dolphy were already well out in front of many contemporaries, and the mutual support demonstrated during their brief time together is beautifully realized here. On A Love Supreme (fascinatingly, recorded a couple days after Live In Seattle), Coltrane leads a kind of crossover group, with Tyner, Garrison, and Jones as the core quartet, joined on the tour by Sanders and Donald Garrett on bass, with Carlos Ward jumping in on sax at Coltrane’s invitation. Both Coltrane and Sanders add percussion along with Jones’s drumming, and if Offering represents some kind of approaching end point in Coltrane’s art, the Seattle performance of “A Love Supreme” leads in the same direction, ever forward. items.body: Label: Burning Ambulance Records, 2026 Personnel - Wadada Leo Smith: trumpet; Sylvie Courvoisier: piano (#1,3); Marcus Gilmore: drums (#1,3); Bobby Naughton: vibraphone (#2-5); Lamar Smith: electric guitar (#2,3,5); Bill Laswell: electric bass (#3,4); Melvin Gibbs: electric bass (#3,4); Mauro Refosco: percussion (#2,3,5); Brian Jawara Gray: percussion (#2,3,5); Pheeroan akLaff: drums (#2-5). Trumpeter and composer Wadada Leo Smith assembled various ensembles for his new album, Constellations and Hemispheres , rooted in harmonic intensity, open structures, and modal depth. The project was sparked by quantum physics, parallel universes, and shifting dimensions, in a no-nonsense approach that explores timbre and atmosphere with serious intentions and exceptional versatility. The album kicks off in trio format, with Smith joining forces with the quick-witted pianist Sylvie Courvoisier and adaptable drummer Marcus Gilmore on “ Dark Energy ”. Cymbal activity is paired with sparse piano texture, while Smith's declamations extend from sharply piercing to dolefully lugubrious. This mournful reflection swells and intensifies via Courvoisier's phenomenal work, expanding and contracting by way of intricately coiling patterns that work as a perfect foil for Smith's obscure idioms. Gilmore is granted a brief unaccompanied passage. " Lake Tanganyika " emerged from a sextet session with trumpet, vibraphone, guitar, percussion, and drums. Ancient, water-surrounded landscapes are evoked via the emotionally powerful lyricism brought by Smith over Bobby Naughton's gossamer vibes and Pheeroan AkLaff's gloriously relentless drum flow. The seasoned drummer also gets our attention on the closer, " Meditation on Love ", a cosmic, open-ended manifesto of peace and hope. Smith traces a spiritual and artistic connection with the Rastafari—associated with the reggae music of Jamaica—but I'm unable to spot that influence here. Yet the music is able to knife through the speakers like a lightning bolt. " Dark Matters, Particles of Light, Mirror of the Unseen " is a full-length workout clocking in at 22 minutes. Powerful and moody, the piece is bookended by the same trio that had shaped the opening track, expanding in its middle part into an octet featuring two distinguished electric bassists, Bill Laswell and Melvin Gibbs, who contribute to the dismal, apocalyptic scenario with authority. A lighter, tactile percussive quality appears by the end, relieving the pressure. The two bassists are also prominent on " Deep Canyons on Mars ", diffusing ominous vibes through gravelly distorted sounds. The heavy, nightmarish tones are pacified when vibraphone and trumpet step forward, yet obscurity still lives here when the bass returns with wah-wah bluesy sounds drowned in electronics. Though the result of multiple sessions, Constellations and Hemispheres feels like a unified experiment—mostly stripped down of gloss but still with haunting and transcendent moments to reflect upon. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Dark Energy ► 02 - Lake Tanganyika ► 03 - Dark Matters, Particles of Light, Mirror of the Unseen
items._cn_summary: Wadada Leo Smith 新专辑以量子物理、平行宇宙为灵感，通过多个不同编制乐团的组合，展开关于音色与氛围的实验。三重奏以稀疏钢琴与镲片活动烘托小号的尖锐与悲怆，钢琴家 Courvoisier 以盘旋音型与小号的晦涩语句形成对峙。六重奏段落借颤音琴的缥缈质感与鼓手 AkLaff 的持续律动，勾勒水域环抱的远古意象。长达 22 分钟的同名曲由三重奏扩展为八重奏，两把电贝斯以权威感塑造阴郁末日图景，末段则以轻盈的打击乐质感释放压力。另一曲中电贝斯以失真粗粝声线扩散不祥氛围，颤音琴与小号的浮现暂时缓和紧张，回归时则融入电子化的哇音蓝调语言。整体虽源于多次录制，却在情绪与美学上保持统一。

items.body: Thematically, Post Dub Cities hearkens back to Future Sound of London’s Dead Cities, while tonally it recalls Murcof’s Rememberanza. Adriano Zanni‘s vision of a future world is the cold reflection of a present reality in which many places are already deserted: peeling houses, dilapidated storefronts, bombed villages. At one time, they teemed with life. Once humans have no more use for a city, they abandon it, leaving only rubble and questionable specters. The reasons may be as far afield as the loss of jobs, the evaporation of resources, or a campaign of bombs. More than anything, Post Dub Cities is an album of mood. Zanni wants his listeners to be uncomfortable, to regard these cities as one does the stone wreckage of Ozymandius. From the opening notes of “Crisopoli” (also the first single), he casts a spell of resignation and despair. The pace is slow, but not sluggish; the beats restrained, but not soft. Someone has to bear witness. In “Pyramiden,” the tone grows harsher, with amplified whispers, clacking pipes and cavernous echoes. Were it not for the dub timbres, one might call this industrial or post-industrial music. Each piece seems to hide another piece behind it: a subdued rhythm, a moving shadow. In “Centralia,” sharp beats stumble like scavengers sifting through wreckage. These visitors may not be human, or even humanoid; in Alan Weisman’s classic The World Without Us, everything from roaches to raccoons reclaims its own. Rust abrades metal; girders bend; branches break through glass. The accompanying pdf is essential to the release. Referencing Calvino and Marcelli, Zanni writes of the empty city as an “echo chamber,” an image reflected in the music. A hundred pages of sublime black and white photographs follow, captured in cities around the world over the past two decades. The unifying feature is the lack of any human presence, as if scrubbed from existence (insert sci-fi theory here). Proof of humanity’s presence remains, but without context. In Zanni’s own words: “memory without recollection, structure without use, body without inhabitants.” In response, the music is architectural: one imagines a grid in which beats and notes are purposely placed. Belgrade, Vienna, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Dublin, Sarajevo, Rome, London, Prague, Madrid, Krakow, Istanbul, Lisbon, Palermo and more, all deserted: buildings empty, rollercoasters stilled, markets abandoned, art left to dissolve. Not a single vehicle is visible, even on the highway. One can see what humans have done, but not where they have gone. In what seems to be the final image, a massive wall of chairs is ready for a group of patrons who never arrive. Capturing these images must have required remarkable patience and timing. The last bonus track, “San Zhi Pod City,” offers a surprise: the appearance of a human voice. Even this turns out to be a loop, a remnant, an echo. But Zanni does have a final trick up his sleeve: on page 99, the people reappear, filling the square. The last four images show humanity wall to literal wall: perhaps too much humanity, suggesting a reason for its removal or demise. As much as one pores through “Kadykchan” and “San Zhi Pod City” for a matching restoration, one cannot hear it in the grooves. The listener is left to ponder whether the detritus of humanity might hold any intrinsic value, or if it is only sound and fury, signifying nothing. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: Adriano Zanni 的《Post Dub Cities》以冷峻的氛围电子为骨架，融合 dub 节奏与工业噪音质感，描绘一座座被遗弃的未来城市。专辑节奏缓慢但并不迟滞，节拍克制却不柔弱，合成器低鸣与管状回响交织，形成废墟般的声场。每首曲目似在另一首背后潜藏线索：压抑的律动、移动的阴影、蹒跚的脉冲。随附 PDF 收录全球废弃城市二十年间的黑白摄影，与音乐互为镜像——建筑犹在，人类缺席。终曲中出现的人声实为循环残响，印证「记忆无回忆、结构无用处、躯壳无居民」的核心意象。

items.body: In Passage, some of the most elemental transitions are embraced and explored using sound to portray some complex and undefined spiritual concepts. The concept behind Passage is that of passing from one phase of your life to another. This may include new residences, changing relationships, traveling to an entirely different solar system, or passing on from this life to whatever may be next. This strange dark new place possibly extends forever Passage by Chris Meyer's Alias Zone featuring Robert Rich   Alias Zone is the cinematic tribal electronic music project of Chris Meyer of Learning Modular. Chris combines unique sounds crafted on his modular synthesizers with field recordings, hand percussion, and other elements in a unique, melodic fashion. I would tell you that the cavern here has no bottom, instead the earth is hollow, there are the sounds of very few strange forces moving about, these are their stories. In Passage, some of the most elemental transitions are embraced and explored using sound to portray some complex and undefined spiritual concepts. The concept behind Passage is that of passing from one phase of your life to another. This may include new residences, changing relationships, traveling to an entirely different solar system, or passing on from this life to whatever may be next. Each slowly-unfolding piece is its own cinematic journey, inviting you to explore Alias Zone’s dreamscapes and imaginary worlds. This time, for Passage, Alias Zone features ambient music legend Robert Rich, who began building his own analog modular synthesizers in 1976, when he was 13, and later studied computer music at Stanford‘s CCRMA while researching lucid dreaming. Working in a wide array of the arts and with over 40 albums spanning four decades, his all-night Sleep ​Concerts opened up the performance of audio arts into a fundamentally whole new dimension. Robert Rich‘s solos on Passage illustrate a series of slow, meditative journeys featuring lush, organic landscapes and waterways, which weave their way through Alias Zone‘s backdrops of quiet industrial decay. Emerging shadows convey powerful stories from the biggest caverns. For Passage, Chris has chosen his custom modular synthesizer, Korg Wavestation, ASM Hydrasynth, Folktek Nano Garden, gong growls, slow-motion rattles & bells. Robert brings his Haken Continuum with eoWave Metallik Resonator, Vibraslide guitar, PVC flute, Expressive E Osmose. This strange dark new place possibly extends forever. Let us commit to continue into the perfect darkness. We are just entering the cavern, the way is dark and we are the first after all these centuries. The old cave has a huge deep pool, the spirits take the forms of water sprites, naiads and undines. I cannot see anything, but I can hear so much, here we are at peace and in balance. Somehow things move slowly when they are this big. The first ceremony has already begun and it continues. “Elegy” (12:13) sets the opening trajectory, we are in the great hall leading to the abyss. After the ceremony usually the previously hidden inner being affirms the change. What I know for sure is that strange things can happen deep in these caves, we can listen and then let them rest. I hear the calls of eyeless creatures of the darkness, I think that all the water spirits are still here, but with a new message. Things get more complex, we are in a sleepy string forest haunted by a theremin-like night rider, “Realization” (17:31) comes into focus. I am dropping a rock into the dark hole and it never hits bottom. After all, we are getting deeper into the cave, travelling for miles and miles. The flute embraces us, and calms us, now it gets quiet. Beyond this place the territory is infinite, and the circumstances change. In the end, the drones melt back into the void. We continue to slowly drift off into oblivion :: The third track, “Horizonless” (15:45) starts, we are hanging out in the bigger cave, there is a construction site in here, too not very close, I hear bubbles swirl, maybe there is deep water, the flute glows, metal tings and rings and the constant listener just floats there. These must be the ancient bells that were once found on the bottom of the old cave. In the  darkness, on a zephyr, the irregular sounds of banging metal clangs in the distance and get loud sometimes. We are kept afloat upon the water sounds and the flute. Who can imagine what they are building out there? We continue to slowly drift off into oblivion. Next we come to “Afterlife (The Three Gates)” (12:58), it sounds like we are passing further down. There is no hurry, I might hear spooky chanting monks beyond the veil. The cenobites are always heading further down into the caverns below, now they are taking us along. Slowly descending. As bowed strings shimmer and echo, I begin to look for signs of the three gates. This must be where the dead people are. Now I know, here is where they keep the real darkness. Chris Meyers has been making electronic music since he was a teenager in the late 1970s. He has designed electronic music synthesizers and digital recording devices for companies including Sequential Circuits and Roland, such as creating the Vector Synthesis sound generation technique. His first album under the name Alias Zone was chosen by AFIM as the best independent electronic/new age album in 2002. The core tracks for Passage came out of an invitation to play a two-hour ambient concert as part of Currents Gallery 826’s Vibrant Pool exhibit, where five different artists – Chris Meyer’s Alias Zone, Jim Coker of Meridian Alpha, Trovarsi, Jason Fink, and Anthony Ballo – performed simultaneously in different rooms of the gallery. Chris recorded his many hours of exploratory improvisations as well as his performance the night of the exhibit, and edited them down to four extended soundscapes. He then passed these pieces on to long-time friend Robert Rich, who notes: “When Chris sent me the raw tracks for his next album, he gave me open permission to try anything. I told him he could delete or modify anything I sent. I responded intuitively, after listening closely to the modes inherent in the pieces, and then charting out harmonic ideas within those pitch spaces. Each piece seemed to ask for a different approach, yet I also wanted to stay somewhat experimental to respond appropriately to the music. I intended my resulting improvised performances to thread between simple and slightly chaotic, to respond to the abstraction in the original tracks.” Robert ended up choosing a Haken Continuum, Vibraslide guitar, PVC flute, and Expressive E Osmose to play over the four tracks. Chris then recorded additional percussion instruments – growl gongs and “slow motion” rattles and bells – on three of the tracks in response to Robert’s solos. The result is a unique collection of sonic worlds which works as an ambient aural environment for meditation or contemplation, as well as for attentive listening and mental exploration. Passage is available on Bandcamp. Passage by Chris Meyer's Alias Zone featuring Robert RichThe post Chris Meyer’s Alias Zone featuring Robert Rich :: Passage (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: In a house in Lomé, a woman kept a set of ceremonial pots she used for preparing potions for the older women of the Vodun temples. Vodun is the West African religion the Ewe and Fon have practised across Togo and Benin for centuries, the one that crossed the Atlantic on slave ships and became Haitian Vodou and Louisiana Voodoo. Its spirits are bound up with natural forces and they are reached through drumming and singing, so those women sang constantly. Her grandson grew up believing all that singing had gone into the clay and stayed there. Years later he took the pots and built a drum kit out of them. His name is Toto Tchilatchi, and half of what Nana Benz du Togo carry onto a stage is those pots. The other half is a bass David Kasanku built out of PVC drainpipe. He used to play bass, then spent four years assembling the gazé tuyau. Once it went underneath Toto’s kit, the pots and drums came to life, and together they made a groove full of sub-bass and complex polyrhythms. That groove became the bedrock for three singers, Lady Apoc, Parus Kekeli and Izealedu, with a small vintage Korg keyboard alongside their voices. The band’s word for what all of it adds up to is trance. They describe Vodun itself as being about rhythm, trance, nature and connection, and Lady Apoc says theirs comes from “repetitive energy.“ None of the five knew each other until 2019, when Peter Solo, the leader of Vaudou Game, came to Lomé to run a workshop and brought local musicians and artists together for it. Out of that workshop came the band, and Solo has produced them ever since. They took their name from the Nana Benz, the wax-print traders of Lomé’s central market who drove Mercedes-Benz cars and were confided in by the powerful. The band say they admire the courage and force those women showed in patriarchal societies. They sing in English, French and Mina, over the Vodun scales of the snake, Dan, and of Mami Wata, about women and the earth, and they say protecting one is inseparable from protecting the other. Their feminism, the band say, comes from the strength and resilience of African women, and their ecology from Vodun itself, and they say protecting women and protecting the earth cannot be pulled apart. Like many people of their generation, they grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun and were taught to be ashamed of parts of it, and at some point they moved away from it. Going back gave them their voice back. They stopped trying to fit into a musical category and started creating from who they are. Even so, they never set out to put Vodun in the spotlight, and years of work in the shadows came before they dared to get on a stage. Their first concert in Europe was Transmusicales de Rennes in 2022, and AGO followed the year after, recorded at the OTODI studio in Lomé with Solo producing. They went back to OTODI in December 2024 to record SÉ NAM, again with Solo, and it came out in June 2025. Its eleven tracks have a more contemporary production and more room for groove and rhythm. The title means “understand me” in Mina, one of the three languages they sing in. In October they bring it to WOMEX in Las Palmas… For this episode of Musical Road to WOMEX they answered our questions about how Vodun meets the dancefloor, what their handmade instruments do and what they hope to find on the island: they want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and find out what traces of African and Atlantic exchange can still be heard in Canarian music, and they arrive, as they put it, with their ears open. The playlist at the end lets you hear what they are bringing. You’ve been described as pioneers of “digital voodoo”. For someone hearing you for the first time, how would you introduce the meeting of Vodun tradition and the dancefloor? For us, Digital Vodou is not about taking something old and trying to make it modern. It is about showing that Vodun is already alive and has always had the power to evolve. Vodun is about rhythm, trance, nature and connection. And the dancefloor can be a place for that too. People come together, move together, let go. We bring traditional rhythms, songs, percussion and the handmade instruments we create into electronic music, bass and contemporary sounds. For us, it is a meeting between something very old and something that is still being born. That is what makes it feel both ancestral and futuristic. The band takes its name from the Nana Benz, the market women who turned the wax-print trade into power and independence. What did diving back into your Vodun heritage, after leaving it behind, open up for you musically? It gave us our voice back. Like many people from our generation, we grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun. There were things we were taught to be ashamed of, so at some point we moved away from it. Coming back to it changed the way we saw ourselves. We realised that Vodun is not only a spiritual tradition. It is also a way of understanding our relationship with the earth, with women, with our ancestors and with each other. And musically, it opened a whole world for us: rhythms, melodies, stories, symbols. Things that were already inside us. We stopped trying to fit into a musical category. We started creating from who we really are. WOMEX lands this year in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, an Atlantic island whose own traditions ride on the timple, a five-string guitar that carries both African and Latin American trade routes. What are you most curious to discover there? We are curious about the connections between the different traditions. Islands are special places. Cultures arrive there, meet, change and survive. We want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and discover what traces of African and Atlantic exchanges can still be heard in Canarian music. And honestly, we are excited about the unexpected. Maybe one of our handmade instruments will meet a sound from the island in a way we never imagined. That is what we love about music. Your instruments are handmade and upcycled, the gazé tuyaux among them, and your themes are feminist and ecological. In a WOMEX programme full of traditions, what makes your sound and your message unmistakably yours? For us, everything is connected. The recycled instruments are not just something you see on stage. They are part of our sound and part of the way we think. We take things that people throw away and give them another life. In a way, we do the same with our stories and traditions. We take things that have been misunderstood or pushed aside and bring them back into the present. Our feminism comes from the strength and resilience of African women. And our connection to ecology comes from Vodun itself. We often say, “Whoever does not respect women does not respect nature.” For us, that says a lot about who Nana Benz Du Togo is. WOMEX is built on unexpected meetings. Which artists, labels or collaborators are you hoping to cross paths with in Las Palmas? We don’t really have a list of names. We want to meet people who are deeply connected to where they come from but are not afraid to experiment. Artists who can move between tradition, ritual, electronic music, performance and new ideas. And that is one of the things we love about WOMEX. You can have a conversation with someone backstage and suddenly discover that there is something you can create together. We are coming with our ears open. You’ve toured Europe and built a reputation as a live force. Does a room of delegates and music professionals change how you bring the trance and the groove of your set? Not really. Of course, we know that WOMEX is important and that there will be a lot of professionals in the room. But once we are on stage, we have to be ourselves. Whether there are one hundred people, a thousand people or music professionals watching us, we want the same thing: for people to feel the music in their bodies. We want them to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and simply become part of the rhythm. That is when the magic happens. “Voodoo is Nature,” you’ve said. Gran Canaria is a volcanic island shaped by the ocean around it. Does a landscape like that speak to the ecology at the heart of your songs? Absolutely. When you see a volcanic landscape, you are reminded that the earth is alive. It is powerful, it changes, it moves. For us, nature is not something outside of us. In Vodun, it is a living presence. The ocean, the wind, the stone, the fire inside the earth, these are not just things around us. They are forces. So being on an island shaped by the ocean and volcanoes feels very familiar to our way of thinking. It reminds us that we are part of something much bigger than ourselves. Your work carries a clear message about women’s strength and respect for the planet. Is there something you feel especially compelled to say through this showcase? Yes. We want to remind people that protecting women and protecting the earth are not separate things. We believe our traditions can still teach us something about that balance. We are not trying to go back to the past. We are trying to understand what we can take from it to imagine a different future. For us, women are creators, transmitters, protectors and forces of transformation. That is something we want to celebrate through our music. After SÉ NAM, what’s next? New recordings, new collaborations, directions you’re keen to push the project toward? SÉ NAM was an important chapter for us, but we already feel the next one coming. We are working on new music and pushing the dialogue between ritual percussion, the instruments we make ourselves and electronic production even further. We also want to work with artists from other parts of Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America. There are so many shared histories, rhythms and spiritual connections across the Atlantic that we would love to explore. We want to keep moving forward without losing our roots. If you could write a personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and discover your showcase, what would it say? Come with your body before your expectations. Come to dance, listen, feel and maybe remember something older than all of us. We are bringing rhythms from Togo, women’s voices, handmade instruments and the energy of Digital Vodou. Don’t just come and watch us. Come and experience it with us. If you join us, we will create the ceremony together.   On 23 October at the Plaza Stage in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Nana Benz du Togo will ask the WOMEX crowd to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and become part of the rhythm   PLAYLIST: NANA BENZ DU TOGO X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Nana Benz du Togo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 这支多哥乐队将伏都教仪式用的陶罐改造为鼓组，PVC水管被制成低音吉他，搭配复古Korg键盘与三位女声，形成充满次低频与复杂复节奏的恍惚律动。乐队从2019年由Vaudou Game主脑Peter Solo组织的工作坊中诞生，以洛美中央市场的Nana Benz蜡染女商人为名，致敬父权社会中女性的勇气与力量。歌词以英语、法语和米纳语演唱，题材围绕女性与大地——在他们的理念中，保护女性与保护地球不可分割。专辑由Solo在洛美OTODI录音棚制作，十一首曲目比此前作品更具当代感，融合西非传统伏都音阶（蛇之神Dan与水之女神Mami Wata）与当代节奏美学，呈现出扎根于地方信仰又超越类型框架的声音实践。

items.body: Band: Sigh | Album: Goh-Ka | Genre: Progressive metal | Year: 2026 From: Tokyo, Japan | Label: Peaceville For fans of: Enslaved, Between the Buried and Me, Opeth Bandcamp Sigh is one of the longest-running and most influential progressive metal bands out there. Starting off as a symphonic black metal band in the early 1990s, they quickly took a more experimental turn and never looked back. Goh-Ka is the band’s 14th full-length release (or 13th, if you want to categorize last year’s re-recording of their 2007 album, Hangman’s Hymn, a little differently). This album is based on kusōzu, a Japanese artform depicting the nine stages of decay described in Buddhism. These are used as a means of meditation on impermanence. The music here sticks to Sigh’s usual style. But where the last album of theirs I listened to–Shiki–left me unimpressed, this is one of their strongest outings. Avant-garde, progressive, and Japanese folk elements play large parts on this album, and the use of recurring musical themes ties everything together. Japanese folk was more prominent than usual on Shiki, and that trend continues here. Goh-Ka opens with the nine-minute “Kuso-shi 1, 2, and 3”. Sigh’s signature synth tones weave and burble amid heavy guitar lines, accented with traditional Japanese instrumentation. This cut is relatively restrained by Sigh’s standards, but that degree of focus pays off here. The power of the music is apparent, and the band’s decision to up the Japonic elements helps this to stand out. The shifts between avant-garde metal, organ-fueled prog, and Japanese folk are fluid and organic. “Jigoku-Zoshi 1: Unkamusho” has an anxious opening with some nearly-Latin-sounding percussion. But soon enough it plunges into melodic black metal with speedy synth flourishes and classical-influenced guitar lines. This is classic Sigh, and it’s a lot of fun. Things slow down on “Anzenshokon”. Acoustic guitar, flute, and clean vocals lend this a mournful feel in its opening. Crushing, doomy guitars burst in on occasion to punctuate the verses, and psychedelic production adds a dreamlike quality, all of which do an incredible job at evoking a corpse rotting in a field, but in a reflective way. In the last couple minutes, the band incorporates obvious early King Crimson influences for a dramatic conclusion. “Kuso-shi 4, 5, and 6” comes next, opening with lush, symphonic doom metal tones. The drumming here (and elsewhere on the album) is stellar, with lots of fancy fills and flourishes. A sinister acoustic passage follows this, evoking some of Opeth’s better quiet moments. Themes from parts 1-3 are revisited here, as are the psychedelic acoustic tones of the preceding song, adding a sense of cohesion. I really like the intermingling of electric and acoustic elements. Not only are Japanese instruments used (maybe it’s a shamisen? Or a koto? I’m not sure.), but some Western-style classical guitar shows up, as well. This is a lurching, foreboding composition that highlights all this band’s best tendencies. “Shoso” is an eerie, one-minute electronic instrumental interlude that leads right into “Unputenpu”. This is a savage, biting composition that sees guitar and shamisen harmonizing beneath raving vocals. Melodic moments contrast against this, and Mikael Åkerfeldt of Opeth shows up to provide a solo. I really love the unorthodox percussion choices deployed during the chorus. Some sinister synth and shamisen open up “Jinmenjushen” as the band dips back into some slower riffage. The verses are much more energetic, though, focusing on melodic black metal, sometimes bordering on black ‘n’ roll. There’s a clear sense of drama here with the group vocals during the chorus, and some unexpected saxophone harmonizes with synthesizer during a particularly exciting instrumental break. This is a breakneck composition that hardly takes its foot off the accelerator once things get going. The final minute does slow down a bit, but there’s no lack of intensity. “Jigoku-Zoshi 2: Tokatsujigoku” immediately bursts forth with powerful black metal. The drumming is again a highlight here. The chorus of this song dips into avant-garde orchestral elements. I’d compare this to some of BTBAM’s odder songs, but Sigh’s been doing weird metal for much longer than those guys. A pair of sub-two-minute songs follow. “Kushukankyo” feels Andean, with breathy flute, gently strummed guitar, and understated hand percussion. It’s a wonderful little breather. “Kuso-shi 7”, on the other hand, consists mostly of sound effects and weird synthesizer bloops.  The album closes on its longest song, the 11-minute “Kuso-shi 8 and 9 / Mettaijakujo”. After a dramatic, theatrical opening, the first verse is relatively grounded. Acoustic and electric passages contrast wonderfully. Dashes of electronic and psychedelic music crop up amid the crushing riffs. Plenty of bands throw things together and hope they work; Sigh is one of the bands that best integrates strange inclusions in a way that makes sense. Folk elements, topped with big, melodic guitar lines lead off the second half of this song. More musical themes from earlier in the record are revisited in a satisfying way. Rock elements eventually melt away altogether as this piece enters its final movement. Orchestral music takes over in a macabre march, eventually dissolving into a synthesizer drone. After some warbling static, the album ends on a warm and peaceful electric piano passage, underscoring the overall concept of this album: accepting the impermanence of life. Goh-Ka is another excellent work from Sigh. Everything here is lively and played with so much passion. The band does an amazing job at varying tempo and texture, and their ability to change direction so suddenly and skillfully is always impressive. Score: 96/100

items._cn_summary: 这是日本老牌前卫金属乐队Sigh的第14张全长专辑，以佛教中的九相图（kusōzu）为概念基础，描绘肉体衰败的九个阶段，作为对无常的冥想。专辑延续了乐队一贯的实验路线，将前卫金属、先锋摇滚与日本民俗音乐深度融合，传统乐器（疑似三味线或古筝）与合成器音色调和交织。作品以系列曲式结构展开，主题动机在多首曲目中反复呼应，形成统一的概念框架。器乐编排上，管风琴驱动的前卫段落与日式民俗旋律交替出现，早期King Crimson式的影响在尾声处浮现。制作方面，迷幻化的声场处理赋予音乐梦幻般的质感，鼓击展现出大量复杂的加花与过渡。整体而言，这是一张在Sigh既有风格基础上强化日本文化元素与冥想主题的概念专辑，器乐水准扎实，融合度高。

items.body: John Coltrane – The John Coltrane Quartet Plays (Impulse, 1965) By Dan Sorrells Most of my listening hours are spent on freely improvised music. But when it comes to Coltrane, I love the classic quartet, 1965, right before things broke open (and the group, apart). The John Coltrane Quartet Plays is what I reach for most often. “Chim Chim Cheree” starts like another “My Favorite Things,” but less than a minute in, Coltrane’s already chafing against the melody, and after two he and Jones are fairly bursting out of Tyner’s measured vamp. “Brazilia” and “Nature Boy” enticingly point toward the searching explorations to come, where ideas were turned inside-out in dizzying, kaleidoscopic epics (something further evidenced by various surfaced recordings from the Half Note during the same period, where “Chim” and “Song of Praise” stretch to twice the length). The sense that traditional song forms must still be made to contain Trane’s increasingly frenetic probing lends indelible tension to the music; these songs are like swelling water ballons, but they’re filled with boiling water. For those of us in the future, it’s all the more heightened when you know just how far things will get pushed, even before the close of the year. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / post-bop / modal jazz / spiritual jazz
items._cn_summary: 这张1965年的专辑记录了Coltrane四重奏在风格剧变前夕的关键时刻。评论者长期沉浸于自由即兴音乐，但对这张经典四重奏作品情有独钟。专辑中'Chim Chim Cheree'以类似'My Favorite Things'的东方调式开场，但不到一分钟Coltrane便挣脱旋律束缚，与鼓手Elvin Jones一同从Tyner稳定的和弦循环中爆发而出。'Brazilia'与'Nature Boy'则隐晦指向即将到来的探索阶段，预示着传统曲式将被内省翻转。评论特别指出同期Half Note的现场录音中这些曲目被拉长至两倍时长。整张专辑的张力来源于传统歌曲结构与Coltrane日益狂热的探索欲之间的对抗——音乐如同注满沸水的气球不断膨胀。对已知后续发展的听众而言，这种张力更被历史视角进一步放大。

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦荷兰低音提琴手Arjen Gorter的职业生涯与音乐脉络。文章追溯了他从手风琴、尤克里里到吉他再到低音提琴的曲折乐器之路，详述了他1966年与Willem Breuker首次合作并录制首张专辑的经过，以及长期担任Willem Breuker Kollektief低音支柱的角色。乐评强调Gorter的独立音乐生涯远不止于Breuker，介绍了1968年他与德国自由爵士萨克斯手Gunter Hampel的合作录音。整篇文章以传记叙事为主，穿插音乐史背景，为听众理解这位欧洲前卫爵士核心人物的演奏风格与艺术地位提供了丰富上下文，体现出对欧洲自由即兴传统的深厚认知。
