items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
items._cn_summary: 这张评论聚焦于集体即兴创作的边界探索，涉及两场二重奏与两场四重奏的录音，跨越十二年时间跨度。文章指出这些作品体现了某种'永恒的边缘'——音乐能够穿透习俗与意义的墙壁，呈现可塑而不可言说的形态。评论详细讨论了Emilio Gordoa与已故Sven-Åke Johansson的专辑《Die Dritte Ebene》，该作品展现出一种近乎透明的品质，仿佛声音中的'另一面'。音乐暗合Erik Satie的家具音乐理念，通过重复素材的特殊共振创造出恍惚而近乎出神的状态，在演奏者之间升起一种反思性的意识。文章强调集体即兴中听者的核心角色：组装、收集、作曲，每个人的诠释都同等重要。这些录音创造出不寻常的空间，使听者能够在回响与共鸣中生成自身的意象。

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.
items.label: ezz-thetics 1070
items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑由鼓手 Gerry Hemingway 领衔，集合德、瑞、日、爱等多国乐手，在瑞士 Altbüron 的 Bau 4 木材工坊录制。评论追溯 Hemingway 与 Anthony Braxton 八十至九十年代四重奏的渊源，指出其当代创作承袭了 Braxton 跳跃式断奏旋律与即兴段落串联的结构手法。专辑以三首长篇作品为核心：双钢琴与鼓的短小即兴穿插其间，三重奏的《Slivers》由巴松管、贝斯与鼓组成，松弛的时间感与低音区的摩擦齐奏呼应了 BassDrumBone 的三人动态；《Bau 4 Assembly》则像一部多线叙事的乐曲，乐手以工坊木屑作为打击材料，在约十分钟处形成轻巧的敲击对话。评论对 Hemingway 的鼓技既肯定其叙事意识，也批评部分段落松弛、收尾主题摇摆感不足。整体评价具体且具技术分析深度。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国-肯尼亚鼓手与八十三岁传统dodo流派歌手合作，是内罗毕独立厂牌的首发作品。制作人用Buchla合成器、手打打击乐与合成多节奏层层铺底，衬托人声而不喧宾夺主。歌曲从简重复的打击动机出发，逐步叠加四拍敲击、低频气泡与木琴质感，最终使电子纹理与原声元素浑然一体。歌手与组合成员在地理与文化上同根同源，抛接唱词时自然带出地域共鸣。评论指出这类跨文化创作的价值在于：传统获得先锋姿态，创新则显出千年根基，全球化语境下非洲离散社群与本土传统彼此回应而不互相抹除。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)
items.label: Bongo Joe
items._genre: world music / Afro-fusion / dance music / Puxa
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了1970至80年代圣多美和普林西比群岛的Puxa舞曲，展示了这一非洲葡萄牙语区小型岛国独特的音乐文化。Puxa融合了来自其他葡语非洲殖民地的音乐元素，混入merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等节奏，加上大西洋对岸加勒比海的影响，形成独特舞蹈音乐传统。评论指出这些岛屿面积很小，录音和发行受限于缺乏城市级别的录音室和厂牌资源，因此现存的唱片尤为珍贵。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队呈现火热的吉他即兴，键盘与贝斯在某些段落退出后，鼓和吉他主导律动，令舞者陷入狂热。多把吉他相互交织、主唱与和声互相呼应，旋律框架丰富，某些现场曲目显然延续数小时。专辑由Bongo Joe小厂牌发行，是非洲边缘岛国音乐档案的重要补充。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 与意大利作曲家 Paladino 及诗人 Ferrari 合作的专辑《Songs of Compassion》收录十一首歌曲。音乐以钢琴为核心，叠加弦乐、木管、合成器音色层与失谐声响，结构非线性和无调性，打破西方和声运动的惯常逻辑，呼应 Steve Reich 与 Philip Glass 的简约重复美学。歌词兼具诗意与政治锋芒，《Pale Wanderer》审视极权主义的合谋机制，《Charlottesville》（与已故 Joe Byrd 合写）直接引用新纳粹口号反讽种族纯洁论，同时延续1960年代抗议歌曲传统并融入对死亡与宇宙位置的冥想。Moskowitz 的演唱摒弃常规旋律走向，以意识流方式逐字展开语义，钢琴则充当另一声部如希腊歌队般评论叙事。整体在实验声响中承载严肃社会议题，是一次跨代际的实验音乐延续。

items._cn_summary: 奥伦·阿姆巴奇（Oren Ambarchi）的新专辑《Cooked》历时三年、横跨三大洲五个国家录制，由十三位音乐人参与，演奏包括尺八、口哨、便携管风琴以及爵士领域的各类乐器。最引人注目的是经过高度处理的人声出现。专辑仅包含两首作品，但并未因元素堆叠而显得过熟，反而呈现出香槟瀑布般的精妙平衡。评论强调这种平衡本身就是专辑的美学核心——每一位演奏者、每一件乐器都在整体织体中占据恰如其分的位置，构成一个有机的整体。这张作品适合对当代实验音乐、多元乐器融合以及即兴创作感兴趣的听众，其跨文化与跨风格的制作方式本身就体现了声音探索的野心。

items.body: Achachay is what highland Ecuadorians say when the cold catches them, arraray when the heat does. Both words came into Andean Spanish from Quichua, and BRITTA builds “Achachay” on the pair: a love song about wanting someone enough to feel both. A requinto line, the small high-tuned guitar of Ecuadorian string music, runs over percussion drawn from the country’s Pacific coast and a trap low end. The alt-pop production leaves the guitar exposed and the beat holds a steady pressure under a vocal that stays at the point of anticipation. Born in Ambato in the central Ecuadorian Andes and based in Los Angeles in the US, Britta has been feeding Ecuadorian traditional forms into dance production for a while: on her single “NON3 (no te dejes avecilla)” she sampled her own voice singing an albazo, the fast triple-time song form of the Ecuadorian highlands, and built a house track around it. “Achachay” points that same working method at Latin alternative, with the Andean Spanish idioms running through the lyric carrying as much of the song’s identity as the requinto and the percussion do. Listen to “Achachay” HERE The post Daily Discovery: BRITTA – Achachay appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 厄瓜多尔裔洛杉矶音乐人BRITTA将安第斯山区传统requinto小吉他、太平洋沿岸打击乐与trap低频底鼓编织在一起，构建出一首以alt-pop为外壳的跨文化情歌。歌词取材于克丘亚语借词"achachay"与"arraray"，分别形容寒冷与炎热，借此隐喻渴望某人时冷热交织的情绪。vocal悬停在期待临界点，与持续施压的节拍形成张力。此前她在单曲中曾采样自己演唱的albazo快三拍高原曲调并制作house曲目，此作延续同一工作方法，将安第斯西班牙语习语作为身份标识置于与传统器乐同等地位，是一次将地方传统植入当代电子语法的扎实尝试。

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — A south Korean group that took 18 years to release their first album and the least one can say isthat Superstring didn't take the easy road. Yes their main influence is classical music, but theywouldn't name have named their kids Ludwig, Johan Sebastian or Wolfgang Amadeus. They might havethought of Edgar, Karlheinz or Gabriel, though. BTW, it's not just about modern classical , as thereare hints of jazz dispersed throughout the duration of their first works. Noteworthy, TGD was firstreleased as vinyl-only, waiting some three years to finally release it in the user-friendly formatcalled CD.Indeed, while relatively dissonant, SS is not extreme Avant Prog like Guapo would be, but they'renot very careful about your sanity beyond your eardrums. Their Grand Design is still relativelyaccessible, if you like atmospheric improvisation, almost cinematic, gloomy ambiances with also PostRock moments. This instrumental quintet will be remarkably stable throughout their career, focusingon the violin and piano as lead instruments, but backed up by a guitar. There are some lovelymoments, but also plenty of tense passages, not necessarily providing a release outlet for thenervous accumulation.TBH, not my cup or tea, but it's definitely worth their Bandcamp detour at least once, even if itwill never be an essential piece of work. Add another half-star, though !!!

items._cn_summary: 韩国乐队Superstring耗时十八年才推出首张专辑，以小提琴与钢琴为核心乐器，辅以吉他构建纯器乐五重奏。作品深受当代古典音乐影响，融合爵士即兴元素，呈现电影化的阴郁氛围与后摇滚段落。专辑最初仅以黑胶形式发行，三年后才推出CD版本。乐评指出其虽具不协和性，但并非极端前卫，保持了一定可听性。作品中存在紧张段落缺少释放出口的问题，整体偏向氛围化即兴，偶有动人时刻但未能成为必听之作。作为韩国独立厂牌的小众制作，带有非西方视角的当代古典探索色彩。

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — SS's second album certainly starts in a WTF, but if Elements of Architecture stretches their TGD debut by a mile, and go the extra-distance to play on the dissonance frontier, but never crossing it. BTW, they must have a fascination about construction design, since their next three releases will mention it on the record sleeves. On the sonic front, it seems that Kim's bass guitar is playing a more prominent role than previously - especially on the title track. In a general way, Kim seems to be the head honcho, handling design & mixing/production, even, if the album is released again on the violinist Dancing Butterfly label. In some moments, via the guitarist, King Crimson is not far away.Definitely a harder grasp on what SS tried to do in this Avant-Post-Prog creation, but if all tracks were more in the mould of Floating Debris, then then they might've gotten that fourth star. .
items._cn_summary: SUPERSTRING 的第二张专辑延续并拓展了首作的不和谐美学，将音色实验推向前沿但未越界，整体偏向先锋前卫摇滚的解构路线。贝斯手 Kim 的演奏占据了显著比重，尤其是同名曲目中低音线条主导了结构走向，他同时负责整体设计与混音制作，乐器编制中可见小提琴这一非摇滚常规元素。某些段落经由吉他声部透出 King Crimson 式的不安张力，但整体处理更为克制内敛。评论者认为专辑风格较难一次消化，作品质量尚未达到前作《Floating Debris》的水准，遗憾地止步于三星。作为一支持续关注建筑意象的乐队，此作已展现出对声音空间感的独特追求。

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Third album in three years after taking 18 years to create their first one, Architecture might sound/read like a logical successor to their previous one, but there is quite a sonic progression here;eve,n if SS' collective paws are plainly recognizable. Indeed, we've taken a steep turn away from Avant-Prog, but I"m not sure this is due to the new arrival Katie's saxophone on three tracks, because it doesn't really change the overall soundscapes, even if the energy reach a different level and intensity - for the better, I might add. But indeed, the general sonic direction of this album tells us that we are at a corner of the band's career.The dissonance element present in their first two albums has almost disappeared, and this helps the accessibility o�f their music. Relatively absent from their first two album, there is a sense of drama permeating most of the tracks, endearing us to their musical escapes and extravaganzas. Emotional melodies over tight rhythms. BTW, it was their first album directly sold in CD, and for both formats, SS took the carte to make an attractive sleeve with a transparent protecting plastic sleeve. TBH, I really don't know why the band will change its name and record label (I guess the departure of their violinist played a big role), after the release of their best-yet album . But there will be two undeniable links: the Architecture link (purposely misspelled) and the same type of line-up (new violinist) and a now-permanent sax player replacing the too-discreet guitarist. but that's for their next album. In the meantime, their third is definitely the one I preferred at the time.
items._cn_summary: 这是乐队沉寂十八年后第三年推出的第三张专辑，相比前作在声学方向上有明显演进。前两张作品中突出的不和谐元素在此作中近乎消失，音乐的亲和力显著提升，戏剧性氛围贯穿多首曲目，情感旋律与紧凑节奏交织。萨克斯手Katie参与三首曲目的演奏，为整体音色注入新能量，强度与张力有所提升但未根本改变声响景观。小提琴手离队后乐队经历更名与厂牌变动，新阵容以萨克斯取代原先过于低调的吉他手。专辑是乐队首次直接以CD形式发行，封面设计配合透明保护塑封。这是一张在可听性与先锋性之间寻求平衡的作品，延续了乐队可识别的声响特征，同时呈现出阶段性的转折。

items.body: Ductape Faded Flowers Swiss Dark Nights Turkish duo Ductape have been gathering a following on the basis of a steady stream of singles and albums, in a very of the moment sound. More than anything, the duo of Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray have found a style that sits between the gloomy darkwave of She Past Away and the more light fast-moving quirky post-punk that we’ve come to associate with Molchat Doma and their ilk, with a touch of modern electro-darkwave for taste. And while their latest LP Faded Flowers is certainly very au courant in terms of the songwriting and performances, there’s also no denying that the band have a talent for it. Listening to cuts like “Figures” or “Gölgesiz” should give a good idea of Ductape at their most straightforward; there’s a strong propulsive bassline backed by stiff kicks and gated snares, plenty of tremelo’d guitar lines and the charismatic vocals of Güleray, who imbues her low moans and whoas with plenty of muscle. It’s a sound the band never stray too far from, but keep fairly fluid, adding in some synth leads (as on the zippy “Delilik”) or touches of other styles (the italo-infused intro of “Burn”) to taste. And while the record does have a certain sameyness to it, it’s fast-moving and has enough switch-ups to keep things moving, such as placing the occasional combo-breaker like the oompah-cabaret stylings of “Velvet Dawn” into the middle of the album. That said, the band’s bag of tricks has its limits, and multiple listens will show some of their weaker tendencies. A big one would be their general production sensibility: the bass and guitar sounds don’t vary much, their drum programming leans on eighties drum machine toms for fills to the point of distraction, and Güleray, for her confidence and power always sits in the same place in the mix, always up front, never varying in dynamics or range. To that point, these songs are often short of an actually memorable hook, usually relying on simple repeated keyboard licks or a simple refrain to fill the role. The fact is that even on multiple listens songs will tend to melt into one another, with only a few really standing out by virtue of having a vastly different tempo or arrangement. “Sad Gravity” is perhaps the most interesting song simply by virtue of using some more fully-fleshed out electronics and touches of spanish guitar. You can see why folks would enjoy a record like Faded Flowers, it’s got a sound with proven appeal, performed expertly and with enough verve to wallpaper its musical shortcomings. Having it on is never unpleasant, and it’ll no doubt have folks dancing at your local goth club, but there’s simply not enough substance here to rise above perfectly fine. Ductape are a band that probably have a really good record in them, and it’ll be interesting to see how they get there from here. Buy it. Faded Flowers by Ductape The post Ductape, “Faded Flowers” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 土耳其二人组合Ductape的专辑《Faded Flowers》延续了当前暗潮与后朋克复兴的浪潮，风格介于She Past Away的阴郁暗潮与Molchat Doma式的轻快后朋克之间，并融入现代电子暗潮元素。强劲的贝斯线配以生硬的鼓机和颤音吉他，Çağla Güleray低沉有力的嗓音贯穿始终。专辑保持紧凑流畅的节奏，偶尔通过合成器主旋律、意式迪斯科元素或夸张的卡巴莱风格段落打破单一感。然而，制作手法相对固定——贝斯与吉他音色变化有限，鼓机过门频繁，混音中人声位置始终不变——导致歌曲间缺乏足够的辨识度与记忆点，整体偏向安全成熟但缺乏突破。

items.body: Tear a piece of this and shove it hard into your mouth A lilylicker sounds like a particularly devoted suck-up, someone whose admiration has become a full-time occupation. Put the word beside Oscar Wilde’s fascination with actresses Lillie Langtry and Sarah Bernhardt, and a whole society of worshippers comes into view: flowers, flattery, beautiful women placed upon pedestals. Wilde was a cunning linguist, of course, though Patriarchy have a few suggestions about putting that talent to more practical use. The lily remains a lovely flower, of course, though its innocence becomes somewhat harder to maintain once somebody starts licking it. The Los Angeles snuff-pop duo of Actually Huizenga and AJ English, otherwise known as The Drummer, premieres the video for Lilylicker, taken from their new EP, Appendices. Written and produced by Huizenga and English, the song takes its initial inspiration from Wilde’s devotion to those celebrated performers, then puts the woman receiving all that attention in charge of the proceedings. A menacing bass synth and a blunt kick drum set the terms, leaving Actually’s near-whispered vocal close enough to feel conspiratorial. Her poetic purr slips between the beats before the track opens into a metallic industrial-techno rhythm, bringing the hard physicality of ’90s industrial into contact with contemporary darkwave. The bass keeps its grip while crushed guitars tear through the chorus, making the move from intimate persuasion to open command feel deliciously abrupt. The words play a similar game. Wanting to be liked becomes wanting to be licked; affection, appetite, and obedience get tangled in the same exchange. Actually moves from seeking approval to prescribing exactly how it should be delivered, with an impatience that gives the song its humor. For all the literary ancestry, the central proposition is straightforward: admiration should have practical applications. Directed by Patriarchy and shot by Hazel Hill McCarthy, the video makes that business of putting people on pedestals unusually literal. Figures revolve on small platforms against an almost uninterrupted black background, their costumes and gestures exposed by direct light. Actually appears in a white gown holding lilies, in a pale pink dress draped with chains, and in a metallic corset with enormous gold wings and a guitar. English handles a skull while wearing little white wings; their young son appears in family tableaux and as a cherub perched on a classical column. The arrangements suggest devotional statues brought to life by people with their own ideas about sainthood. There is an affectionate absurdity to these living ornaments. The solemn poses give way to movement, expressions change, and the family portrait keeps interrupting the fantasy of immaculate statuary. Against all that black space, the slightest human detail becomes conspicuous. Even the insects have supporting roles. The setting came about through necessity. According to the band, the owner of their original studio location objected to the proposed content and the presence of their son, who was also appearing in the video. With the shoot abruptly displaced, the crew relocated to the Angeles woods and rethought the production outdoors. Huizenga subsequently edited the footage “happily alone and for many hours,” describing editing as “one of my secret pleasures.” “I decided not to retouch anything either. So all razor bumps, dark circles, cellulite, and sock lines are fully visible if you wish to judge me physically… I had a baby, so kill me! The boys are perfect though. A lot of the things that went ‘wrong’ ultimately added to the beauty of it, like having to shoot outside, where moths kept flying in front of our lenses, drawn in by the bright lights” For Huizenga, leaving those imperfections intact also connects to Patriarchy’s larger, apocalyptic view of power: “Patriarchy has never been about perfection, it’s about realizing we are the last remnants of human existence before AI enslaves us all; that’s why the project is called Patriarchy after all, patriarchy is the final human ruling order. Our next masters wont be women or men or human in any form, so we need to embrace our chaos and imperfections while we can.” Watch the video for Lilylicker below: Released in the wilting days of this past Summer, Appendices brings together five songs developed across different periods of the band’s life, reaching back to The Unself sessions and forward through the aftermath of 2025’s Manual For Dying. These recordings have survived abandoned versions, rewrites, and changes substantial enough to turn industrial tracks into orchestral ballads and minimal synth into metal. Alongside Lilylicker, the EP includes Bite Marks, Servile, Ode (to an Apprehensive Tyrant), and Hate Fuck, with additional production and mixing contributions across the record from Ben Chisolm and Matia Simovich. Huizenga’s reading supplies another connection between these otherwise unruly songs. Wilde, Marchesa Luisa Casati, Emperor Tiberius, and the Manson family furnish starting points for examinations of sexuality, submission, obsession, and violence. Across three full-length albums, a live record, and numerous remixes, Patriarchy have pursued those interests through industrial electronics, synth-pop, metal, and performance art. Appendices also documents Huizenga and English becoming an increasingly self-contained production team, with Lilylicker pointing toward the club without surrendering their taste for theatrical excess. That appetite for the personal and the unruly carries into Actually’s Sex and the Pity, Huizenga’s new podcast and livestream concept, whose pilot is announced for this Friday at 10 p.m. Pacific. Pitched as Elvira meeting Gore Vidal, it promises secret guests, fireside conversation, and previously untold stories from Patriarchy’s tours and beyond, forming a living journal for a future film project. “I can only really seem to recount these hilarious stories properly when I’m talking one-on-one with a cute gay at a party; so I’m gonna try to recreate that free-form energy for the podcast.” Listen to Lilylicker below and order the Appendices EP here. items.body: Los Angeles-based ambient explorer stanleycypress finds comfort in smaller spaces with Ephemeral, a two-track slice of life where atmospheric modulations weave through melodic drone tones and cascading Detroit-inflected textures. A melancholic intersection of sound and space Los Angeles-based ambient explorer stanleycypress finds comfort in smaller spaces with Ephemeral, a two-track slice of life where atmospheric modulations weave through melodic drone tones and cascading Detroit-inflected textures—think Rod Modell—across opener “Momentary Drift.” “Trillium,” meanwhile, doubles down on duration and amplitude, its minimal techno and Plastikman-like tentacles revealing a 3 a.m. 313 soundtrack for wandering souls. Isolated highs hover above drowning low-end, before an eventual breakdown gathers every microscopic element and gradually energizes it through its closing minutes, pulling the listener deeper into its hypnotic current. Two tracks steeped in ambient techno propulsion, calm, and control; one piece reflecting another. Together, they form a melancholic intersection of sound and space, a flow that feels just right at just over ten minutes, yet could easily drift infinitely. Ephemeral is available on Bandcamp. Ephemeral by stanleycypressThe post stanleycypress :: Ephemeral EP (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 洛杉矶环境探索者stanleycypress在这张仅含两首作品、总时长约十分钟的EP中，以紧凑篇幅铺陈出沉静而深远的氛围。开篇曲将大气调制与旋律性嗡鸣交织，融入底特律式的层叠质感，呈现出忧郁而克制的情绪肌理；后续作品则延展时长与振幅，以极简技术与简约的脉冲节拍推进，塑造凌晨三点的迷幻漫游感。高频漂浮于低沉低频之上，最终在收尾段落中逐渐将微观元素汇聚并积聚能量，将听者引入催眠般的声流。整张作品以环境技术的推进力为基础，融合嗡鸣与极简主义逻辑，在短小篇幅中构建出既可循环又似无尽延伸的空间感。自发行于Bandcamp，属于独立小厂牌范畴，无主流商业气息。

items.body: In August of this year, New Focus Recordings released New Music for Two Voices, an impressive collection of acapella vocal music by sopranos Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest. This lavish album features a full hour masterful singing of six contemporary works, including three world premiere recordings. Susan Narucki is an accomplished soprano who has appeared as a soloist with the Cleveland Orchestra, Los Angeles Philharmonic, the San Francisco Symphony, among many other international appearances. She is presently on the faculty of the Department of Music at UC San Diego. Kirsten Ashley Wiest is an award-winning coloratura soprano who has performed and recorded alongside numerous GRAMMY winners, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, San Diego Symphony, Bang on a Can All-Stars and the Partch ensemble, among many others. Kirsten currently teaches voice at San Bernardino Valley College and University of California Riverside, New Music for Two Voices is a deep dive into the cutting edge of virtuoso vocal technique as it intersects with contemporary musical composition. The album is accompanied by excellent liner notes, full translations of the texts and biographical notes on the composers and the performers. The outstanding sound engineering is by Andrew Munsey and Kristina Tran. The first track on the album is come sempre (2025), by Dutch composer Rozalie Hirs. Although written just last year, the liner notes inform that this piece “…evokes music of an earlier time, with shifting tonal centers and interwoven melodic lines..” Running at over 7 minutes, it is one of the longer works of the entire album and is a world premiere. come sempre features two voices singing separately in Italian, sometimes together and sometimes in a call and response pattern. The vocal lines are often independent and weave in and around each other seamlessly in a series of lovely harmonies. There is no accompaniment anywhere in this album so the two singers must rely on their internal sense of rhythm and pitch. Where crisp phrases are present, these are always clean and punchy. Nothing ragged or blurry here; the notes are precise and balanced. As the piece proceeds it gradually increases in complexity, summoning ever greater technique. The singing by these two confident voices, however, is always controlled throughout. The poems of El trino persistente by Javier Tafur González are the inspiration for TRINOS, a series of twelve miniature works by Colombian composer Alba Potes. Commissioned by Susan Narucki in 2024, all are less than one minute long, yet these pieces sparkle like brilliant gems. The liner notes state that “Each of the twelve settings seems to capture a moment in time—by turns, lyrical, nostalgic, jubilant, hopeful.” “TRINOS: I. Jazmin” is the first of the twelve pieces and although less than a minute in length, it sets the standard for the precision and vocal technique that is heard throughout the entire work. A high vocal tone opens, then falls rapidly in pitch as a second voice joins in a middle register with dissonance. The singers must rely on their own intuition for pitch and timing – there are no accompanying chords or common rhythms. The overall feeling is one of welcome and portent. Although less than a minute in length, this first piece sets a high bar for vocal artistry. Other pieces in the work are similarly concise and illustrate the consistent level of virtuosity brought to bear by Wiest and Narucki. “TRINOS: II. Entra illuminando la casa”, at just 32 seconds in length ,is intense, with many jumps and leaps in the two voices. It shines like a fiery jewel. “TRINOS: IV. No saldré” features a middle register voice together with a lower voice in close harmony. Stretches of unusual dissonances challenge the singers, but are navigated successfully. “TRINOS: VI. Timida flor” opens with a strong voice soaring up very high with impressive power and good control. “TRINOS: VII. Ven, anclemos” is soft, with almost mournful feeling and quietly sentimental. The text, even in English translation, is perfect: “Come, let us anchor now hands entwined.” “TRINOS: IX. Se hundió el buque” by contrast, is completely different. A quiet, solo voice is heard in a middle register, reserved and subdued. The lyrics are more spoken than sung, producing a purposeful and deliberate sensibility. “TRINOS: XI. Podemos estar juntos” is another solo piece with a strong voice crying out as if in sadness. The singing here is expressive, yet delivered with great clarity. The final piece in the work is “TRINOS: XII. En los hilos”, a duet with the lower voice in sustained tones underneath a soaring, coloratura voice. The dissonances in the harmonies add a powerful, melancholy feeling to this. TRINOS is a masterful collection of small pieces that each deliver an emotional punch from the virtuosity of the performers. The third work on the album is From the Grammar of Dreams (1988), by Kaija Saariaho and consists of five pieces based on two separate texts from the American poet Sylvia Plath. The liner notes tell us that “The five duets demonstrate Saariaho’s unique compositional language, with its attention to fine gradations of vocal color, intricacy and flexibility of gesture, and a nearly overwhelming range of emotional expression.” The first duet, labeled simply “I”, opens with strange and painful sounds in the lower voice with struggling vocals in the second voice as if forcing out the words and notes. Leaps and jumps are heard in the upper voice accompanied by sustained and plaintive sounds from the lower. Just a little over 2 minutes long, this piece is expressively weird and haunting.“II”, the second piece in From the Grammar of Dreams begins with two sets of spoken words heard simultaneously. This is somewhat chaotic as there is no common tones or phrasing. One voice includes some rather gruesome details, as if recounting a nightmare. The voices are alternately speaking and singing and often very agitated. The music is complex and dynamic, yet confidently delivered. The third duet, “III” is soft and melodic; completely different in character from the previous pieces. There is lovely harmony in the two voices with lots of sustained notes and dramatic gestures. There is a welcome and mysterious feeling to this. “IV” opens with scratchy, breathy sounds followed by strong vocal music. The voices jump and soar as each part bounces breathlessly off the other. The two voices devolve in a sort of shouting match just before the piece concludes with a few short breaths. Amazing technique here. The final duet, “V”, begins with a series of sustained notes in both voices sung in a high register with prominent vibrato. The sounds loop around each other independently in pitch and dynamic. This produces an eerie feeling at times but is mostly strongly declarative. The fourth work on the album is NauðaR Níu [The Nine Needs] (2025), by Jeffrey Holmes. This collection of nine pieces is based on old Norse Runic carvings (ca. 5th through 12th century), as compiled and translated by the composer. As with the other works in this album, each piece is short, ranging from 37 seconds to a little over three and a half minutes. As explained in the liner notes, NauðaR Níu features some unusual accompaniment: “Throughout, the vocalists play a variety of percussion instruments; the sound of metal, skin, wood and natural materials contributing to the sense of a vast primeval landscape.” The opening piece of NauðaR Níu, titled simply “I”, starts with soft tones by two voices. As this one minute piece proceeds, a gentle gong sound and some light percussion are heard; a subtle and mysterious beginning. “II” sets a completely different tone. A sharp drum rap begins, serving as a starting exclamation point. The two voices weave in and around each other in sustained tones amid much howling and spooky vocals. Another series of bangs from the drum and a woodblock add to the unnerving atmosphere. “III” returns to a more settled and soothing feeling. A low sustained vocal in one voice is made more expressive by the light tinkling of chimes. Very mystical and solemn with lovely vocals and reverential sentiment. “IV” continues in a sacred feeling, opening with an Ahhh sound in a single voice. Another voice joins in, accompanied by quiet gong tones and a low drone. The exotic – almost Asian – feel of this is supported by devout vocals, gentle chimes and percussion. “V” continues in the exotic groove and returns to the more forward style with drum raps and sharp woodblock beats. The voices seeming to chant with out words but in eerie, sustained tones. There is a decidedly spectral and anxious feeling to this. “VI” returns to the more subdued refinement heard in “IV”, with a soft opening and chimes. A sudden drum strike with wood block recalls the mood in “II”. A gong is heard between the sustained and almost mournful vocals. There is a sacred, worshipful feel to this. “VII” continues with chimes and a high, plaintive opening vocal. The top voice soars in very high, airy sweeps. More chimes accompany. The excellent singing, heard in very high registers, is controlled, on pitch and does not lose its power. “VIII” opens with a strong drum strike and woodblock rap. Loud, almost screaming vocals are heard, as if in great surprise. A palpable sense of danger and fear is present. Loud drum and woodblock strikes accompanied by long, descending sweeps of vocals paint a convincing musical portrait of fear and despair, This sets the stage for the final section, “IX” which opens with a haunting vocal solo , soon joined by the second voice in call and response. The voices are subdued with somber descending pitches and accompanied by drum strikes, chimes and gong strikes. All elements of the various sections seemingly combine into a sense of acceptance and fateful resignation. Beautiful, expressive singing is heard as the vocals fade to the finish. With NauðaR Níu, Jeffrey Holmes has forged a vibrant musical connection between the Old Norse culture and our own.The next work on the album is a collection of five short pieces titled Two Walking (1994) by French composer Pascal Dusapin. The text for Two Walking is by American writer Gertrude Stein and the work was originally conceived by Dusapin as a study for his chamber opera To Be Sung. The opening piece of Dusapin’s collection, titled “I. How many little wings” begins with a single lyrical voice followed closely be a second vocal, almost as an echo. Now the higher voice soars in a sustained upward arc with text following in both voices. The vocals bounce and dance around each other, evoking birdlike acrobatics on the wing. As the tempo increases the text becomes louder and more frenetic. A sudden slowing towards the finish provides the listener with a soft landing. “ II. Kiss my lips” begins with a quiet clicking and two voices in a sort of conversation. There is a whispering and intimate feel to this, sung as if in secret. “III. May, June” opens with a long solo note followed by the second voice entering slightly below in a counter melody. Now the notes in each voice volley back and forth effectively. As the text moves faster, crisply sung in short, quick phrases, the result is a pleasingly complex texture that does not sacrifice the beautiful harmonies. “IV. A scene in singing” has both voices starting together but soon singing separate lines. Short snappy phrases are heard in places and at times the harmony is unusual, but the overall effect is both lovely and abstract. The final piece in the Dusapin work is “ V. It seems to be”. Two voices in lower register open in syncopated rhythms and the separate vocal lines produce an engaging, crunchy texture. The pitches and harmony are controlled and balanced, even with the lively phrasing. “ V. It seems to be” is a fine finish to an intriguing work. The concluding work on the album is Melisande (2022), by Marti Epstein, the longest piece at almost 13 minutes. Inspired by the Debussy opera, Epstein re-imagines the story as if told through Melisande’s own experience, rather than as a reflection of others. In this interpretation, “the two sopranos alternate between extending and finishing each other’s words, functioning as a single unit, or singing passages with overlapping, contrapuntal lines that give way to moments of ecstatic release.” Melisande opens with two sustained voices in a delicate harmony and dynamics that vary intriguingly. The vocals become more active, with independent lines weaving in and around each other in a call and response pattern. By 4:10 the voices are singing in common phrases in an effective contrast to the opening. The upper voice is especially impressive, exhibiting a fine tone with strength and confidence. By 7:10 the vocals are in solid harmony and declarative text sung expressively in middle registers. The lines diverge and become occasionally independent, one often following the other. The duet singing here is especially disciplined and precise. At a slowing of the tempo, Melisande fades quietly to its finish. An excellent performance of technically challenging music.New Music for Two Voices is a dazzling exploration of vocal virtuosity that sets – and meets – a very high standard. Hopefully this premiere album by Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest will be the first of more to follow. New Music for Two Voices is available in digital download or CD format from: Bandcamp:HB Direct: The post Susan Narucki & Kirsten Ashley Wiest – New Music for Two Voices appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Review by tedfromtoe — If you like a combination of symphonically arranged instrumental music with a dose of avant/RIO style, then I recommend this album. It includes members of two instrumental bands from Spain. Two members are from the symphonic styled Kotebel and one member is from the more chamber/avant/RIO/jazz styled October Equus. I've been a long-time fan of both Kotebel and October Equus (mostly their first three albums) and this did not disappoint. After this album was released in early 2026, later that year, the same label (Vessence Experimental) re-issued their first effort ("Triptych") which was originally recorded in 2016 and previously only available to subscribers of their fan club. "Triptych" apparently does not include the member from October Equus, so is more symphonic and restrained, but very nice.

items.body: Review by Deadwing — Terrifying angels is PRR 4th album after their comeback, with another fantastic release! (4th in arow if you ask me!)They are back to a heavier sound, after the softer and more reflective Coming Up to Consciousness.Still, there are a lot of new experimentations, and it is their proggiest album in the discography,especially due to the 2 larger tracks. The production/mixing was done by Bruce Soord which is shownin a beautiful and balanced composition: the guitars sound heavy but also very crispy with tightsounding and the drums are beautiful and probably the best mix in their discography.All the trademark elements of PRR are here: Heavy and groovy guitars, very grunge and industrialsounding, distorted soundscapes, eletronic passages and multi-layared vocals.Standout tracks are Black-Arrow Acrobats and Hold Your Wrath, featuring unexpected turns, ambience,creative chord progressions and build ups. Spin Like Fire and Haywire Heart are explosive rockingstandout singles. Rumination Ruin is an excellent companion to the sublime title track and BelowRadiance is a more electronic piece with a beautiful composition and ambience.
items._cn_summary: 这是英国前卫摇滚乐队 Pure Reason Revolution 复出后的第四张专辑，被乐评视为其最具前卫探索精神的一张作品。相较前作更为内省的氛围，新专辑回归到更具冲击力的厚重吉他音色，同时融入了工业电子元素与多层次人声编排。制作与混音由 The Pineapple Thief 主脑 Bruce Soord 操刀，呈现出饱满而清晰的低频与颗粒感分明的吉他层次。专辑中两首长篇曲目贡献了主要的前卫骨架，配合多首紧凑单曲，形成了从炸裂摇滚到电子氛围的多变走向。电子段落、失真音景与出人意料的转调贯穿始终，是一张在传统摇滚框架内持续拓展声音边界的作品。

items.artist: Live review: Agonoize, System Noire & Antibody

items.body: There was a useful logic to the running order of Friday night’s show at Klub Łącznik. Antibody, Agonoize and System Noire all make music designed to work physically, but they approach that physicality from quite different directions. Antibody built movement through rhythm and the almost compulsive momentum of hard electronic dance music. Agonoize converted it into confrontation, theatrical violence and direct exchange between performer and crowd. System Noire then expanded the same basic principle into something broader and increasingly combustible, combining electronic force with the dynamics of a full band. The evening became an accumulation of different ways of controlling a room. The concert was part of the 2026 run pairing Agonoize with System Noire, with Antibody as special guest; for System Noire, the tour also marks the Hanover band’s 10th anniversary. The Wrocław date was officially scheduled at Klub Łącznik, the concert space within Czasoprzestrzeń at the former Dąbie tram depot. Antibody Photos: Karo Kratochwil Antibody opened the evening, and first a small correction worth making because the name is easily mangled: the project is the work of Jan Laustroer. Laustroer began Antibody in 2013, when he was only twelve, and over the following years developed a sound drawing on industrial, power noise, dark electro and the harder end of rave and hardcore. The debut album Opera of Death appeared in 2017, while the more recent Never Quite Right was released in 2024. In January this year Antibody also collaborated with Grendel on “The Ranidae.” What worked especially well in Wrocław was that none of this required the opening slot to pretend it was already the climax of the night. Antibody’s set was extremely danceable, rhythmically insistent and immediately mobile. The tracks worked through repetition, sharp changes of pressure and bass strong enough to make the body respond before there was much reason to analyse what was happening. It was energetic without becoming shapeless; Jan understands that hard electronic music needs more than volume and speed if it is supposed to sustain movement. The visual presentation supported that. Against a star-filled background, the recurring frogs added a deliberately absurd signature to a set otherwise built around hard, mechanical momentum. They have become an immediately recognisable part of Antibody’s visual vocabulary, and after this year’s Grendel collaboration The Ranidae, their presence felt even more appropriate. There was something rather charming about the collision: pounding industrial rhythm underneath, a small amphibian mythology unfolding behind it. As an opener, Antibody did exactly what was needed. The set did not simply “warm up” the audience in the conventional sense; it established movement as the evening’s basic mode of communication. By the time it ended, the room was no longer waiting for the main acts. Agonoize Photos: Karo Kratochwil The change was immediately visible when Agonoize came on. The space in front of the stage became noticeably denser, bodies moved closer together, and the kind of dancing established during Antibody’s set turned into something more collective and more aggressive. Agonoize were formed in Berlin in 2002 and have spent more than two decades making the relationship between harsh electronic music and extreme stage performance central to their identity. Their current touring page explicitly designated the Wrocław concert as a “Blutshow”, continuing the use of theatrical blood that has long been part of the band’s live language. Their most recent full studio album remains Revelation Six Six Sick, released through RepoRecords in April 2021. Calling what happened at Łącznik simply “brutal” would miss why the set worked. The force was carefully organised. The electronics were dense, abrasive and extremely physical, but they also retained enough rhythmic definition for the material to still work as dance music. Chris L.’s performance depends heavily on this ambiguity: he confronts the audience while simultaneously demanding its participation. And participate they did. The stage blood is obviously theatrical, but the reaction it produces is real. Chris repeatedly showered the front of the audience with it, leaving faces and clothes streaked red, and the people closest to the stage seemed delighted to become part of the spectacle. The distinction is important. Agonoize’s blood show does not function particularly well when treated as something happening to a passive crowd. In Wrocław it became reciprocal. People moved forward knowing very well what was coming. They danced harder, reached towards the stage and quite visibly enjoyed being pulled inside the performance. That made the visual violence feel less like decoration attached to the songs and more like an extension of their physical logic. Chris’s gestures were large and confrontational because the music required a body capable of matching its exaggeration. The show continually crossed the line between concert and grotesque theatre without allowing the theatrical element to weaken the musical one. The encore shifted the visual vocabulary again. Chris returned wearing wings, and after so much aggression, blood and pressure, the image had a surprisingly different weight. It was beautiful precisely because the evening had not prepared us for beauty in any conventional form. The wings did not suddenly turn the performance sentimental; they introduced another register into a stage language that had spent most of the set emphasising impact and provocation. My conversation with Chris afterwards changed how I thought about the performance even further. We had previously discussed his long absence following a very serious illness, but hearing him describe the extent of the recovery in person gave that history a different scale. He spoke about having to rebuild abilities that most people never consciously think about, including basic everyday tasks and forms of recognition, through an exhausting rehabilitation process. I would not want to turn illness into an inspirational narrative imposed on the concert, because that would reduce both the person and the performance. But it does change the meaning of what one has just witnessed. Returning to a stage is one thing. Returning to this kind of stage presence, where the performance demands constant physical engagement, vocal force, timing, theatrical control and the ability to command a densely packed room, is something else. The striking thing was not simply that Chris was back. It was the absence of caution in the performance. In our recent interview, he told me that he has nothing to prove to anyone except himself and that what he wants, fundamentally, is simply to continue making music. Watching this set, that statement became much less abstract. The stamina was visible, certainly, but more important was the appetite behind it. This did not look like someone tentatively reclaiming an old position. It looked like someone fully inhabiting it again. System Noire Photos: Karo Kratochwil If Agonoize generated the evening’s most theatrical violence, System Noire converted the accumulated energy into something broader and, by the end, almost unruly. The Hanover project was founded in 2016 and is celebrating its tenth anniversary this year. Its current formation has grown beyond the original electronic core, and the band’s recent material increasingly allows guitars and a harder industrial-metal edge to interfere with its dark-electro and EBM foundations. Their 2024 album Aftermath includes ten tracks and was followed in February 2025 by Lost Control, whose single version the band themselves describe as harder and more guitar-driven, while a separate club edit strips it back towards electronics. That tension between programmed precision and a more volatile live-band attack was exactly what made the final set work. By this stage the audience no longer needed persuading. Smoke filled the stage, the lighting became much more aggressive, and the room that Antibody had initially taught to move and Agonoize had pushed into increasingly physical participation now had very little reserve left. System Noire used that. Their music has enough melodic architecture to keep the songs readable even when the performance becomes extremely dense. That mattered here. The combination of electronics, forceful vocals, percussion and the heavier edges of the current sound could easily have collapsed into undifferentiated volume; instead, the rhythmic centre remained very clear. People could dance to it. The lighting and smoke also worked unusually well with that construction. They were not merely there to make the stage appear “dark”. Smoke repeatedly altered what could actually be seen: musicians emerged, disappeared and reappeared as the lights cut through it, creating a visual equivalent of the music’s own alternation between defined melodic lines and heavier blocks of sound. And gradually the whole thing became wonderfully disorderly. By the final part of the set, the dancefloor was no longer behaving like a room of individuals politely occupying their allotted space. Movement propagated through it. People were dancing hard, responding to the band and to one another, and the distinction between observing the show and physically participating in it had largely disappeared. Calling it carnage is not much of an exaggeration, although it was an exceptionally friendly form of carnage. System Noire therefore made sense as the final band, even though Agonoize might initially appear the more obvious dramatic climax. Their set did not need to out-provoke what had come before it. Instead, it took the accumulated kinetic energy of the entire evening and gave it somewhere to go. Klub Łącznik Photos: Karo Kratochwil Klub Łącznik itself deserves some credit for why the evening felt so comfortable despite the intensity inside. The venue sits within Czasoprzestrzeń at the former Dąbie tram depot, and its layout provides something particularly useful for this kind of scene event: a clear separation between the physical density of the concert hall and the open area outside. Inside, there is a proper concrete-floored club space where a hard-electronic show can become as loud, smoky and physically crowded as it needs to be. Outside, the yard changes the social rhythm completely. Between sets people could step out, cool down, talk, meet friends and, importantly, encounter the musicians without the strange separation that larger venues often create between audience and performers. That mattered more than it might sound. A night involving three relentlessly physical electronic sets can become exhausting when there is nowhere for the intensity to dissipate. At Łącznik, it could. The outside conversations, pauses and meetings with the bands gave the evening breathing space, while every return indoors felt like deliberately re-entering the pressure. Three approaches, one increasingly crowded dancefloor What I liked most was that the evening had progression without needing an artificial concept imposed on it afterwards. Antibody made the body move through rhythmic precision and rave-derived momentum. Agonoize turned the same physical response into confrontation, participation and grotesque theatre. System Noire then took an audience already pushed far beyond passive listening and drove that energy through the dynamics of a full, forceful live set. The crowd grew thicker, sweatier and considerably bloodier as the night progressed, but the atmosphere never became hostile. Quite the opposite. There was a great deal of warmth underneath the noise: people dancing, talking outside, meeting musicians, returning inside and throwing themselves back into it. And perhaps that is the detail worth keeping. With music this aggressive, the obvious vocabulary is always brutality, darkness, violence and impact. All of those things were present. What made the Wrocław show successful, however, was how much pleasure there was inside that aggression. Antibody looked playful behind the pounding rhythms and wandering frogs. Agonoize turned theatrical bloodshed into something the front rows actively wanted to share. System Noire finished with smoke, light and enough accumulated movement to make the floor feel barely contained. By the end, Klub Łącznik looked appropriately wrecked, and the people inside it looked extremely happy. About Agonoize, System Noire and Antibody Agonoize formed in Berlin in 2002 around vocalist Chris L. and have built more than two decades of work around harsh electronic music paired with extreme, theatrically violent stage shows. Their most recent full studio album, “Revelation Six Six Sick,” was released through RepoRecords in April 2021; Side-Line marked that release with a streaming concert announcement at the time. Earlier releases include the 2019 EP “Blutgruppe Jesus (-) / Schmerzpervers 2.0” and the album “Midget Vampire Porn.” Ahead of the Wrocław date, Side-Line interviewed Chris L. about returning to the stage after a serious illness and new material. System Noire, from Hanover, were founded in 2016 and marked their tenth anniversary in 2026. Side-Line first profiled the project in a 2017 Face The Beat feature. The band’s sound has expanded from its original electronic base to include guitars and a heavier industrial-metal edge, documented on the 2024 album “Aftermath” and the February 2025 single “Lost Control.” Antibody is the project of Jan Laustroer, who began releasing music under the name in 2013 at the age of twelve. Side-Line introduced Antibody in a 2016 Face The Beat profile and later featured the track “Secrets” as a 2019 free download. Laustroer’s debut album, “Opera of Death,” followed in 2017, with “Never Quite Right” arriving in 2024. In January 2026, Antibody collaborated with Grendel on “The Ranidae.” Agonoize, System Noire and Antibody played Klub Łącznik, the concert venue inside the Czasoprzestrzeń cultural centre at Wrocław’s former Dąbie tram depot, on September 25, 2026.

items.body: 040118180514 and 102119200914. No, these aren't the result of my cat stepping on my keyboard; they're pseudonyms for the members of Endspace, an experimental black metal duet hailing from Canada, who have been constantly reinforcing their "sci-fi black metal" sound through a trail of releases leading up to their debut record—or "transmission", per the record's pattern of naming each song as a sequential broadcast. Whatever is contained within First Contact, it's going to be alien as hell. As predicted, First Contact is hypnotizingly strange. Dissonant metal genres are already on another plane of disorientation, but Endspace ramp the perplexity up tenfold, via the myriad synths, electronics, and vocoders at the duo's disposal, mostly implemented in their "singing". 040... and 120...'s vocals genuinely sound like extraterrestrial communications. After thirty-nine minutes however, the gimmick gets tiring. In fact, the second transmission alone exemplifies how overpowering their incomprehensible "vocals" can be. Across the nine transmissions, the "vocals" range from the pitch of a dog whistle to murky, gurgly depths, and once—during "Seventh Transmission"—can you pick up a robot warning the "system engaged." Everything, including that excerpt, is also always too loud for whatever mood First Contact is currently in, with zero instrumental tracks providing a much-desired break. "Ninth Transmission", is a particular offender, being constructed in a repeating calm/harsh pattern, and the recurring blasts have a high chance of blowing an eardrum or two.It sucks, because underneath the alien mess that are the vocals, Endspace play commendable dissonant and technical black metal. The streak from the "Seventh" to "Ninth" transmissions, plus the chug-centered niceness that is "Third Transmission", all feature guitar-forward, chaotic deliciousness, whose overhaul of electronics donates a symphonic feel to the record. This helps the otherworldly atmospheres, with the positively overpowering climax of "Fourth Transmission" providing the pinnacle of symphonics. Elsewhere, keyboard lines sound like opera notes and any synth undertone majorly assists any song it's found in. The tracks without a metal attitude, however, leave room for the aforementioned annoyances that are the vocals. The "Second", "Fifth", and "Sixth" transmissions are the definite weak spots in First Contact, with the fifth leaning too much into a noisy electronic beat.While the execution of First Contact was as experimental and wacky as I hoped it'd be, I bit off way more than I could chew with this LP. Tinny, vocoded emanations bury rather pleasing metal, resulting in a listen that I'm not anticipating returning to anytime soon, and doesn't further my desire for Endspace to make a second acquaintance. First Contact by ENDSPACE

items._cn_summary: Endspace 来自加拿大的实验黑金属二人组，首张专辑以九首「传输」为架构贯穿整体概念，融合大量合成器、电子音效与人声变调器，将传统黑金属的嘈杂与不协和推向更极端的异化方向。评论指出其器乐层面具备值得肯定的失谐黑金属技术性，吉他驱动的混乱段落与交响化氛围铺陈构成亮点，键盘声部亦有歌剧式的层次感。然而人声处理过度使用vocoder效果，从超声波频率到含糊不清的电子喉音始终贯穿全作，第二、五、六首传输尤为薄弱，且全专缺乏器乐间奏段落导致听觉疲劳。评论者最终认为实验概念虽有趣，但执行上过于饱和，掩盖了金属部分的潜力，整体未能构成令人反复聆听的完成度。

items.body: John Coltrane – Live at the Village Vanguard (Impulse, 1997) By Kenneth Blanchard There are certain recordings that stretched my grasp of jazz (and indeed music). Andrew Hill’s Point of Departure comes to mind. Coltrane’s LVV collection is another. Recorded over four nights in 1961 at the Jerusalem of Jazz, only five of the originally recorded numbers were released in the following two years. The 1997 box set is a genuine treasure. The structure of the music remains within standard hop bop spaces, but the moods blossom into an entirely new ecosystem. The inclusion of Eric Dolphy was one of Trane’s most brilliant moves. On Naima, Spiritual, India , his low horns (also sax and bass clarinet) perfectly match Trane’s tenor and soprano sax. Trane’s interest in alternative spiritual and musical traditions is obvious enough. His famous “sheets of sound” slide in and out of every line. I find the articulation of Coltrane’s own personality to be as vivid here as on any of his recordings. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / spiritual jazz / avant-garde / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张合集收录了John Coltrane 1961年在Village Vanguard四个晚上的现场录音，其中仅有五首在随后两年内发行，1997年全集的发布让完整面貌得以呈现。音乐结构仍植根于bebop框架，但情绪氛围拓展为一个全新的声学生态系统。Eric Dolphy的加入是这张唱片的关键，低音乐器——包括中音萨克斯、次中音萨克斯与低音单簧管——与Coltrane的次中音与高音萨克斯形成层次丰富的对话。Coltrane对非西方精神传统与音乐传统的兴趣在这套录音中体现得十分充分，其标志性的"声幕"技巧贯穿每个乐句。与Andrew Hill的《Point of Departure》一样，这套唱片被作者视为拓展其爵士乃至整体音乐认知边界的重要文献。
